title: Are boys or girls taller in this Grade 5 section?
description: The mean and the median heights of boys, girls and the whole class of a second Grade 5 section are compared, and then set beside the first section. The video shows why one class cannot decide who is taller.
teaching_notes: One idea: compare groups by their means and medians together, and be careful about claiming a rule from one class. Watch for students who say boys are taller everywhere after seeing one section.

source: Dot plots of heights of another section of Grade 5 students: observations and inferences from the means and medians
video_script.why: The child can read a mean and a median and now uses both to compare boys and girls, and two sections.
video_script.substitution: Put the means side by side, then the medians, then each mean against its median.
video_script.anchor: Second section, heights in cm: whole class mean 141.21, median 142.5; boys mean 142.05, median 143; girls mean 140.14, median 140.
video_script.payoff_line: In this section the boys are taller on average, but in the first section the girls were.

final_answer.value: this section boys taller on average; first section girls taller; first section taller overall (144.5 against 141.21 cm)
final_answer.spoken: the first section mean is one hundred and forty four point five against one hundred and forty one point two one

maths_rules: this section: boys mean 142.05 and girls mean 140.14; 142.05 - 140.14 = 1.91, about 2 cm
this section: boys median 143 and girls median 140; 143 - 140 = 3 cm
boys mean 142.05 < median 143; whole class mean 141.21 < median 142.5; girls mean 140.14 is close to median 140
first section: girls mean 146.9 and boys mean 142.94, so girls were taller there
first section whole class mean: (2430 + 1616) / 28 = 144.5 (the book prints 144.4); 144.5 > 141.21
video_script.design: One idea: compare groups by mean and median, and do not turn one class into a rule. Two sets of three labelled dot plots sit in the anchor, one set for each section.
